metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Equipment lead times for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling systems, and accelerators now stretch from years rather than months, making them as critical a constraint on data center construction as permitting itself.

The supply chain for electrical infrastructure has become the binding physical constraint on AI's power supply. A transformer ordered today may not arrive for years. This delay directly translates to delayed facility completion, which delays power delivery, which delays compute deployment. No permit or financing moves faster than the equipment that must be installed.

This metric matters because it reveals where the bottleneck has shifted. Two years ago the constraint was regulatory approval. Now it is manufacturing capacity and logistics for equipment that few suppliers produce at scale. For an industry trying to double compute every year, a two-year lead time on a single component can slip an entire facility's schedule.

The data covers order-to-delivery timelines for core electrical and computing equipment. It does not quantify how many projects are delayed, by how many months, or whether lead times are lengthening or stabilizing. It also does not break down which equipment classes drive the longest delays, or whether new suppliers are entering the market to reduce them.
